newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. calls Cyprus talks extremely cordial.
newsitem.headline: U.N. calls Cyprus talks extremely cordial.

text.p: Leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities had extremely cordial talks in New York last week, but the moment of truth would come at their second round of talks in Switzerland next month, a senior U.N. official said on Monday.

"I found the atmosphere excellent, and people who are Cyprus-ologists tell me that the discussions were unprecedented in their cordiality," said Diego Cordovez, who headed the talks as Secretary-General Kofi Annan's special adviser for Cyprus.

Cordovez, Ecuador's ex-foreign minister and a former U.N. under-secretary-general, was briefing reporters on four days of meetings between President Glafcos Clerides, as leader of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, at a rural resort called Troutbeck, 90 miles (145 kms) north of New York city. The talks ended on Saturday.

"I saw real good faith, good will, a commitment to negotiate. They both told me, jointly and separately, that they thought Cyprus might be destroyed if they didn't reach an agreement," Cordovez said. "I want to dispell any notion that they are not interested in an agreement."
The Ecuadorean diplomat, who has 25 years' experience as a U.N. official, headed negotiations in the late 1980s that led to the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Afghanistan.

He said the atmosphere at Troutbeck was so good that Clerides and Denktash -- long-time friends and adversaries who had not met for nearly three years -- themselves decided to discuss a number of humanitarian issues on their return to Nicosia, even though it was politically sensitive for them to be seen together there.
Cordovez said they had agreed in principle to a second round of talks in Switzerland, beginning Aug. 11. Another source said that session might be held near Montreux.

"That will be the defining moment," Cordovez said, since the two leaders would come with reactions to suggestions he had made about the way sustained negotiations should be conducted after presidential elections are completed in Greek Cypriot-led southern Cyprus next February.
He had not made any suggestions regarding the substance of the issues themselves.
Cyprus has been partitioned since troops from Turkey took over more than a third of the island in 1974 in reaction to a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
The United Nations has been trying for decades to reunite the island as a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.

Instead of following previous attempts to work out a preview agreement that would then be turned into the legal documents of a comprehensive settlement, he had suggested that "they should take a short-cut...and go straight to the legal instruments," Cordovez said.

"Now it is going to be an incremental process where they draft a number of things, they agree on a number of things, and when they come back they take it from there," he said, adding that nothing would be finally agreed until everything had been agreed.

After Cordovez briefed Security Council members earlier, council president Peter Osvald of Sweden said they were "very pleased to learn that these talks were held in a positive and constructive atmosphere."

In a statement to reporters Osvald added: "Security Council members urge the leaders of the two communities to uphold a sustained process of direct negotiations until the instruments that will constitute a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue have been concluded."

Council members also urged the two sides to "respond constructively to the suggestions made by the secretary-general's special adviser on Cyprus so that further progress can be made at the next round of talks."
Denktash said in a statement in New York the talks were "a positive first step in a new settlement process."

This was an opportune time for the U.N. and the world community to act "as we face the imminent threat next year of the deployment of Russian missiles by the Greek Cypriots," he said, referring to the planned installation of S-300 air defence missiles.

Denktash said the situation would also be destabilised "by untimely action by the European Union" on membership for Cyprus, which the Turkish Cypriots say could only follow a settlement between the two communities.

Despite "painful memories and unjust realities that must be addressed," he added, "we will make every effort to take advantage of this opportunity to represent the aspirations and concerns of our community and to seek reasonable and practical solutions that can bring peace and prosperity to our families and our children."
